Pregnancy

Karyotype testing: chromosomes, pregnancy and other uses

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A karyotype is a laboratory examination of chromosome number and large structural changes. It can answer important questions during pregnancy, after reproductive difficulties, in a child's developmental assessment or in some cancers. The right sample and laboratory method depend on the question; a normal result does not exclude every genetic condition.

What a karyotype examines

Chromosomes package DNA inside cells. Most body cells with a nucleus usually contain 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, with one set inherited from each biological parent; eggs and sperm usually contain 23. A karyotype can identify an extra or missing chromosome and some large rearrangements, such as a piece attached to another chromosome.

This is one kind of genetic test. It does not read every gene or detect every small DNA change. Some rearrangements are balanced, meaning no large amount of chromosome material is gained or lost, but their location may still matter for reproduction. Ask what the requested test can and cannot detect.

Why it may be offered outside pregnancy

Selected investigations for infertility, repeated pregnancy loss or a stillbirth may include chromosome testing of pregnancy tissue, one or both parents, or both. Testing is not automatically needed after every loss. A parental balanced rearrangement can affect reproductive chances, but many losses occur despite normal parental chromosomes. A result is not evidence that anyone caused the loss.

A child with certain congenital differences or developmental concerns may also be offered testing. In some blood disorders or cancers, chromosome changes in affected cells help classify the illness or guide treatment. Such acquired changes are not automatically inherited or present in every cell. A genetics or specialist team should explain the particular reason and whether relatives need assessment.

Pregnancy screening and diagnosis are different choices

Blood screening, including cell-free DNA screening (NIPT), estimates the chance of selected chromosome conditions; it is not a diagnostic karyotype. A higher-chance, nonreportable or otherwise concerning screen, an ultrasound finding, family history or a previous affected pregnancy can prompt a discussion of diagnostic testing. Age can influence chance, but 35 is not a universal eligibility boundary.

After counseling, you may accept or decline screening and diagnostic testing. You do not have to undertake several different screening strategies or an invasive procedure simply because one is available. Ask how the answer would affect care and what alternatives exist. A reassuring screen lowers the chance of the conditions screened for but does not rule out every genetic or developmental problem.

Examples of chromosome findings

An extra chromosome 21 causes Down syndrome; extra chromosome 18 or 13 causes Edwards or Patau syndrome. These conditions have different health and developmental implications. Full trisomy 18 and 13 often involve serious medical needs and a high chance of pregnancy loss or early death, but mosaic or partial forms and individual outcomes vary. There is no single lifespan deadline that applies to every child.

An extra X chromosome, often 47,XXY, is associated with Klinefelter syndrome and variable hormone, learning and fertility needs; assisted reproduction may help some people. Turner syndrome involves a missing or altered X chromosome, sometimes in only some cells, and can affect growth, ovaries and the heart. Most people with Turner syndrome have typical intelligence, although specific learning difficulties can occur. A chromosome label alone cannot predict every person's abilities or care needs.

Blood, other tissues and bone marrow samples

A blood sample is common for a person's own chromosome assessment. Depending on the question, a cheek, skin or another tissue sample may be more informative. Some chromosome changes occur in only a proportion of cells, called mosaicism, so a reassuring blood result may not settle a question involving another tissue.

For selected blood disorders or cancers, clinicians may collect marrow fluid by aspiration and sometimes a small solid core by biopsy. These are sampling procedures, not different types of chromosome analysis. Ask about local pain relief, possible sedation, medicines and any fasting instructions. Do not stop prescribed medicines yourself; arrange another driver if sedation is planned.

CVS and amniocentesis during pregnancy

Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) collects placental tissue using ultrasound guidance through the abdomen or, in some circumstances, the cervix. It is usually performed around 11–14 weeks; specialist guidance advises against CVS before 10 weeks. Amniocentesis collects fluid around the baby with an ultrasound-guided needle from 15 weeks, commonly at 15–20 weeks or later when needed. The team chooses timing and technique for the pregnancy.

The sample may undergo a karyotype, a rapid targeted chromosome test, microarray or another analysis selected for the clinical question. Sampling does not mean every possible genetic condition is tested. Placental findings sometimes differ from the baby's cells, so CVS may require further clarification or amniocentesis. These procedures are not routine methods simply to learn fetal sex.

Discuss sampling risks and preparation

Examining chromosomes in the laboratory does not itself cause a miscarriage; obtaining a sample can carry risks. CVS and amniocentesis have a small miscarriage risk and other possible complications. RCOG estimates the additional miscarriage risk with a skilled operator is likely below 0.5%; multiple pregnancies and individual circumstances need separate discussion. Do not assume one procedure is always safer from a fixed percentage alone.

Ask about the local service's risks, pain relief, infection precautions, recovery and contact number. Discuss blood-borne infections, bleeding problems and medicines beforehand; an anti-D injection may be offered when appropriate for a rhesus-negative pregnancy. Blood sampling may bruise; marrow sampling can cause bleeding or infection. Follow your team's individual instructions rather than changing medicines, food or activity on your own.

What happens in the laboratory

For a conventional karyotype, suitable cells are usually grown and examined while dividing. Specialists stain, count and arrange the chromosomes to look for large changes. Microarray can find smaller gains or losses of material, but does not detect balanced rearrangements in the same way. Neither method reads every gene; targeted or sequencing tests may be needed for a different question.

A rapid targeted test such as QF-PCR examines selected chromosome numbers and is not a complete karyotype. An early rapid result and a later detailed report may therefore answer different questions. Culture time, the specimen and follow-up investigations affect turnaround. Ask which results are preliminary, when the complete report is expected and who will explain it; do not assume all results arrive within three days.

What normal and abnormal results mean

A normal karyotype means no relevant number or large structural change was detected within that test's limits. It cannot guarantee freedom from every genetic condition or predict all future health and development. Small changes, gene variants, low-level mosaicism and changes absent from the sampled tissue may be missed. Sometimes cells do not grow sufficiently and another sample or method is discussed.

An abnormal result may describe a chromosome gain, loss, balanced or unbalanced rearrangement, or mosaic finding. Its importance depends on the exact change, tissue, clinical findings and family context. Further tests or parental samples may clarify it. A prenatal diagnostic result can establish a particular chromosome finding without predicting every symptom or the severity of an individual child's condition.

Planning next steps with support

Ask for a copy of the report and a plain-language explanation of the finding, remaining uncertainty and follow-up. Genetic counseling can address recurrence chances, possible testing of relatives and future reproductive options without pressure. After loss, investigations should be accompanied by compassionate support; deciding whether to test tissue or parents is a shared decision, not a search for blame.

During pregnancy, specialists can discuss further imaging, care after birth and the options available to you if a condition is diagnosed. Outside pregnancy, results may guide a child's assessment or cancer treatment. Decisions should reflect the actual findings and your circumstances. Ask about access, costs, expected waiting time and who to contact while waiting; an app cannot interpret a chromosome report.

After a sampling procedure: when to seek help

After CVS or amniocentesis, contact your maternity team urgently for vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, fever or feeling hot, cold or shivery, contractions, or persistent abdominal pain that is not settling as advised. After marrow sampling, contact the team for fever, increasing pain, redness, swelling, discharge or bleeding at the site. Follow the procedure-specific instructions and do not wait for laboratory results before seeking help.

Seek emergency care for pelvic or abdominal pain that is severe, worsening or painful with movement or touch, or pain with faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy vaginal bleeding or sudden confusion. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Mild expected discomfort does not explain away a warning sign.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask which clinical question the test addresses, what sample and laboratory method are planned, and what a normal result would not exclude.

Discuss consent, alternatives, collection risks, medicines and aftercare with the responsible team; obtain a contact number and result plan before the procedure.

Arrange a results discussion or genetic counseling, and seek urgent help for sampling warning signs rather than waiting for the report.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record appointment questions, sampling dates and the agreed result plan. It cannot analyze chromosomes, confirm a genetic diagnosis, predict a child's abilities or replace genetic counseling and procedure aftercare. Seek clinical advice for symptoms regardless of app notes.

When to seek help

After CVS or amniocentesis, urgently contact maternity care for bleeding, fluid leakage, fever or chills, contractions or persistent abdominal pain. After marrow sampling, contact the team for fever, increasing site pain, redness, swelling, discharge or bleeding. Severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain with movement or touch, or pain with faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy vaginal bleeding or sudden confusion needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself. Do not change prescribed medicines or interpret a result without the responsible team.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A karyotype checks chromosome number and large structure; it is not a test for every genetic condition.
  • Pregnancy screening estimates chance, while diagnostic laboratory testing answers a specific question; both are informed choices.
  • CVS samples placenta, amniocentesis samples fluid, and blood or marrow may be used for other indications; collection risks differ.
  • Normal, balanced, mosaic and abnormal results need interpretation in context, sometimes with another test or sample.
  • Seek prompt help for sampling complications and emergency care for severe or concerning pelvic pain; do not wait for the report.

Frequently asked questions

When might I be offered a karyotype?

It may be offered after a concerning pregnancy screen or ultrasound, for selected infertility or loss investigations, developmental concerns or certain cancers. The clinical question determines whether karyotype or another test is most useful. It is not mandatory for everyone or restricted to people aged 35 and over.

Why discuss chromosome testing after a miscarriage?

Sometimes testing pregnancy tissue or selected parental samples can help explain a loss or guide future counseling. It is not automatically needed after every miscarriage, and a normal parental result does not mean a loss could not have had a chromosome cause. Ask what the result would change and seek support while deciding.

Can it be done in pregnancy, and when?

Yes, using an appropriate sample. CVS usually takes placental tissue around 11–14 weeks; amniocentesis samples fluid from 15 weeks, often at 15–20 weeks. Exact timing and the laboratory analyses depend on the pregnancy and local specialist advice.

Is NIPT the same as a karyotype?

No. NIPT is a blood screening test that estimates the chance of selected conditions. It cannot replace diagnostic confirmation when that is needed. A CVS or amniocentesis sample can be used for different diagnostic methods, not automatically a karyotype alone.

Are there risks?

The laboratory analysis itself does not harm the pregnancy. Sample collection has its own risks: CVS and amniocentesis carry a small miscarriage risk, while marrow sampling can cause bleeding or infection. Ask about the procedure, operator, multiple pregnancy and your own circumstances rather than relying on a universal risk ranking.

Does a normal result rule out every genetic condition?

No. A karyotype has resolution, tissue and mosaicism limits and does not read every gene. Microarray or another test may answer a different question. Even a confirmed chromosome finding cannot predict every future symptom or individual outcome.

How long do results take?

It depends on the sample, cell growth and analyses requested. Rapid selected-chromosome results may arrive before a full karyotype or other detailed report, which can take weeks. Ask which findings are preliminary and agree how the complete results will be discussed.

Which symptoms need help after sampling?

After CVS or amniocentesis, urgently contact maternity care for bleeding, leaking fluid, fever or chills, contractions or persistent abdominal pain. After marrow sampling, report fever or worsening pain, redness, swelling, discharge or bleeding. Severe or worsening pelvic pain, pain with movement or touch, or pain with faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or sudden confusion needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
